operations.description:
Retrieve a single inventory history entry for a specific product variant.

An inventory record is a stock history entry for one product variant. It preserves the business history of how that variant’s stock changed over time and provides a clear trail for review and accountability. This operation returns one exact record by its identifier within the scope of the specified product variant, allowing callers to inspect the quantity change, the reason for the movement, and the timestamp when the change was recorded.

This endpoint is intended for the seller who owns the product variant and for administrators who need to review inventory movement history. The record must belong to the product variant identified in the path; if the record does not exist in that variant’s inventory history, the request must be rejected as not found. The data returned by this endpoint is read-only and represents historical movement information, not the current stock value itself.

Current stock for a variant is derived from the full sequence of inventory history records for that variant. For that reason, this endpoint is typically used together with product variant detail views and inventory history list endpoints when callers need to understand how the current stock position was formed. It does not modify stock, create movements, or recalculate inventory; it only exposes the stored movement entry in detail.
operations.name: at
operations.specification:
Load the inventory record by inventoryRecordId and ensure it belongs to the productVariantId provided in the path.
Use a join or scoped lookup that filters by both identifiers so cross-variant access is impossible.
If the record is missing, or if it belongs to a different variant, return not found.
Do not compute stock here; the endpoint is a pure read of a single immutable history row.
Authorize access for the owning seller of the product variant and administrators only.
Return the full inventory record payload including quantity change, reason, and timestamp fields defined by the schema.

responseBody.description: Detailed inventory history entry for the specified product variant.

parameters.description: Target inventory record's ID within the specified variant.

operations.description:
Update the ordered image collection preserved inside a specific product snapshot.

This operation lets an authorized seller or administrator revise the image set stored for a historical product snapshot while keeping the snapshot bound to the selected product. Product images are maintained as an ordered set, and that order is part of the product’s visual presentation history. The first image in the ordered set represents the primary thumbnail used for product listing presentation, so the stored order must be preserved exactly as provided by the request.

A product snapshot captures the product’s full state at the time of change, including the product’s name, description, category, base price, images, and related variant snapshots. This endpoint works within that preserved historical context rather than on the live product image set. The service must confirm that the snapshot belongs to the product identified in the path before applying any update.

Only the product’s owning seller and administrators may use this operation. The request must be rejected if any image does not belong to the selected snapshot, if an image belongs to another product, or if the image set is otherwise inconsistent. When validation fails, the existing snapshot image order must remain unchanged and no partial update may be committed.

This endpoint is typically used together with product snapshot retrieval operations so that a client can inspect the preserved product state and then adjust the snapshot image ordering or membership as needed for history review or reconciliation workflows.
operations.name: update
operations.specification:
Load the target product snapshot by productId and snapshotId, ensuring the snapshot is scoped to the specified product. Confirm the authenticated actor is either the owning seller for the product or an administrator with cross-product access.

Validate the request body as a complete replacement of the snapshot’s ordered image membership. Every referenced image must exist within the snapshot’s image collection and must not belong to another product or another snapshot. If the request contains any foreign, missing, duplicated, or otherwise invalid image references, reject the entire operation and leave the stored ordering unchanged.

Persist the update inside a transaction so that image ordering and membership remain consistent. If the underlying snapshot image records are stored as child rows, rewrite their ordering fields in a single atomic step, or replace the collection in a controlled transaction that preserves referential integrity. Do not modify the live product image set; only the historical snapshot image records should be affected.

Return the updated snapshot image collection after commit. If the product snapshot is immutable in the broader domain model, treat this endpoint as updating the normalized child image presentation records attached to the snapshot context only, not the snapshot’s preserved product scalar fields. Handle not-found cases for either product or snapshot, authorization failures, and membership validation failures with appropriate errors.

responseBody.description: Updated product snapshot images in preserved display order.

parameters.description: Target snapshot ID within the specified product.
parameters.name: snapshotId

requestBody.description: Ordered snapshot image update payload.

operations.description:
Retrieve a single preserved image entry from a product snapshot.

This operation returns one immutable row from the historical image set captured for a product at the time a snapshot was created. The snapshot image data belongs to `shopping_mall_product_snapshot_images`, while the surrounding snapshot metadata belongs to `shopping_mall_product_snapshots`. Together, these records preserve the product's visual presentation as it existed at the moment the product was edited, including the image URI and the display order used to reconstruct the gallery later.

Access to this endpoint is intended for sellers reviewing snapshots of their own products and administrators reviewing any product history. The server must verify that the requested image belongs to the requested snapshot, and that the snapshot belongs to the requested product, before returning the record. If any identifier does not match the stored relationships, the operation must return a not-found style error rather than exposing cross-product historical data.

This endpoint is part of the product history review flow and is typically used together with the product snapshot detail endpoint and the snapshot image list endpoint. It does not modify data, and it does not expose active product images; it only returns the preserved snapshot-time image information used for audit, dispute resolution, and historical reconstruction of the product gallery.
operations.name: at
operations.specification:
Load one product snapshot image by productId, snapshotId, and imageId.
First verify the snapshot exists and belongs to the product, then verify the snapshot image exists and belongs to that snapshot. Use a single query with joins or chained lookups to prevent cross-snapshot leakage. Return 404 when the product, snapshot, or image relationship does not match.

Authorization: allow the owning seller for their own product snapshots and administrators for any product snapshot. Do not expose this endpoint to customers because it is a historical merchant record.

Use the snapshot image table as the source of truth for image_uri and display_order. The parent snapshot record provides historical context and should be checked for consistency with the product. No write transaction is needed because the endpoint is read-only.

Edge cases: if the image was preserved but the parent snapshot is missing, treat the relationship as invalid and return not found. If the product was deleted after the snapshot was captured, historical snapshot records remain readable as long as the snapshot and image records still exist.

responseBody.description: Historical product snapshot image data.

operations.description:
Retrieve the authenticated customer’s order history as a paginated list of preserved purchase records.

This endpoint returns the customer’s completed and retained orders in newest-first order so the shopper can review their past purchases at a glance. Each summary entry is intended for list presentation only and includes the order number, order date, total price, and overall order status, matching the platform’s order history browsing requirement.

The order history is retained for legal and seller-record purposes even when a customer account later disappears from the active account tables. This means the response must be assembled from preserved order data rather than relying on the current customer profile record. The list must continue to show historical orders exactly as stored, supporting the business rule that past purchases remain visible after customer account deletion.

Access to this endpoint is intended for the owning customer account. The service should enforce ownership at the application layer and return only the authenticated customer’s orders. Pagination should be applied before returning results, and the sort order must always prioritize the newest orders first so the most recent purchases appear at the top of the list.
operations.name: index
operations.specification:
Implement a customer-scoped order history query against shopping_mall_orders, filtered by the authenticated customer identity and restricted to retained orders only. Sort by order creation or order date descending so the newest orders are returned first.

Use pagination parameters from the request DTO to limit the result set and compute the total count consistently for the page response. The summary projection should include only the fields required by the list view: order number, order date, total price, and overall order status. Do not join order item details unless needed to compute the overall status or summary fields.

Ensure the query works when the related customer account/profile has been deleted. The order rows themselves are the source of truth for this endpoint, so the service must not depend on active customer profile existence. If the authenticated principal does not own any orders, return an empty page result rather than an error.

Authorization must enforce customer ownership. Administrators should not use this endpoint for oversight; they should have separate admin-facing order access endpoints. Handle invalid pagination input according to shared list-query validation rules.

responseBody.description: Paginated order history summaries for the authenticated customer.

requestBody.description: Pagination and list query parameters for the customer order history.

operations.description:
Retrieve the shipment tracking information for a specific order.

This endpoint provides the package-level delivery reference that belongs to the order’s shipment record. The shipment stores the carrier name and tracking number as the shared tracking context for all order items included in that shipment, so customers can follow delivery progress from the purchase history and order detail screens.

The response is intended for the authenticated customer who owns the order, while sellers and administrators may access it when their permissions allow inspection of fulfillment records. Because the tracking information is part of the preserved purchase record, the API should return the current shipment tracking state even after later account or catalog changes.

This operation does not expose editable shipment data and does not return order item mutation data. It is a read-only detail lookup that should resolve the order by its identifier, load the related shipment records, and present their carrier and tracking information together with shipment status and timestamps. If the order has multiple shipments, each shipment should be represented as a separate tracking entry because different sellers ship separately and each shipment carries one shared tracking context.
operations.name: at
operations.specification:
Implement a read-only order tracking lookup that loads shipment records belonging to the given order ID. Resolve the order first, verify the requester is allowed to view the order, then query shopping_mall_shipments by shopping_mall_order_id ordered by created_at ascending or by fulfillment relevance if needed.

Return carrier_name, tracking_number, status, shipped_at, and delivered_at for each shipment. If the order has no shipment records yet, return an empty tracking collection or a not-yet-shipped state representation, depending on the response schema design. Do not include order item mutation fields or shipment editing capabilities.

Enforce ownership and access control: the order owner may view the data, and seller/admin roles may view it only when permitted by the platform authorization rules. If the order does not exist or the requester lacks access, return the standard not found or forbidden response from the application layer.

Since tracking information is shared across all items in a shipment, do not attempt per-item tracking joins or item-level carrier overrides. Use the shipment as the single source of truth for tracking context.

responseBody.description: Shipment tracking details for the order.

operations.description:
Force-cancel a platform order and finalize the order’s state for administrative enforcement.

This operation allows an administrator to intervene on an existing order when platform oversight requires cancellation of the entire purchase record. It is part of the administrative order-enforcement workflow and is intended for moderation and policy enforcement scenarios where the platform must override the normal customer or seller lifecycle.

When this operation succeeds, the system updates the affected order and its order items so the final enforcement decision is reflected in the persisted records. Any stock that must be restored as part of the cancellation is returned to inventory, and the resulting order data should be immediately suitable for customer service, seller operations, and administrative review.

This endpoint is only available to administrator actors. It should reject attempts to force-cancel orders that have already reached a finalized state through another action, preserving the existing final status and preventing duplicate enforcement. The response returns the updated order representation so clients can display the enforced result without making an additional fetch call.
operations.name: forceCancel
operations.specification:
Load the target order by orderId, including its order items, shipment state, and current fulfillment/cancellation/refund statuses. Verify the authenticated actor is an administrator before performing any mutation.

Before applying the enforcement action, check whether the order has already been finalized by another terminal action. If the order has already been force-cancelled, force-refunded, or otherwise finalized in a way that makes a second cancellation invalid, reject the request and leave all persisted data unchanged.

If the order is eligible, perform the cancellation in a transaction. Update the order and all affected order items to the cancelled state as required by the business rules for administrative enforcement. For each affected item, restore stock for the associated product variant by writing the appropriate inventory adjustment record(s) or by invoking the inventory service used elsewhere in the platform. Ensure the inventory adjustment is committed atomically with the order status update.

Preserve historical purchase data and snapshots. Do not remove prior snapshots or overwrite preserved purchase-state records. The operation should only update current operational state and add any required audit/history records. If the platform uses snapshots for enforcement decisions, create them as part of the same transaction.

Return the updated order aggregate after the transaction commits. On failure, return a conflict-style error for already-finalized targets, authorization errors for non-admin access, and a not-found error when the orderId does not correspond to an existing order.

operations.description:
Force-refund an order under administrator oversight.

This operation lets a platform administrator enforce a refund on the specified order when business policy requires intervention. It is intended for order oversight scenarios where the administrator must finalize a refund outcome for an order or for an eligible order item within that order, and the system must preserve the resulting order history for later review.

The refund action must honor the platform rules for finalized order states. If the target order or order item has already been completed by another final order action, the request must be rejected and the previous final state must remain unchanged. When the refund is accepted, the affected item state must become refunded, the preserved order history must remain available, and any stock that must be restored by the refund workflow must be restored through the inventory side effects handled by the service layer.

This operation is restricted to administrators because it is part of platform oversight over customer orders. It is typically used together with order detail retrieval and administrative order review flows so that an administrator can inspect the current order state before applying enforcement and then verify the final state after the action completes.
operations.name: process
operations.specification:
Implement an administrator-only enforcement endpoint that loads the target order by orderId, verifies the requester has administrator privileges, and checks whether the order or its relevant order items are still eligible for a force-refund action.

The service must reject the request if the target has already been finalized by another completed order action, including a prior refund, cancellation, or other terminal status that makes a second forced refund invalid. This duplicate-finalization guard is required so the previous final state remains unchanged.

If the order contains a single eligible target item, apply the refund to that item and update the order-level derived state accordingly. If the business workflow allows the entire order to be force-refunded, apply the refund across the relevant items in the order using a transaction so that item status updates and any stock restoration happen atomically. Persist any refund-related decision records and historical snapshots required by the existing refund model so the enforcement event is auditable.

Ensure that stock restoration is performed only for the items actually finalized by the force-refund action, and that the order history remains preserved for downstream order history and dispute review use cases. Return the updated order aggregate after the transaction commits. If the order is not found, return a not-found error; if the caller is not an administrator, return forbidden; if the state is already finalized, return a conflict-style rejection consistent with the duplicate force-refund rule.

operations.description:
Force-cancel a single order item as an administrator intervention.

This operation allows a platform administrator to cancel one specific order item when the business requires direct enforcement. The action is item-scoped and affects only the targeted purchased line, preserving the independence of other items in the same order. It is intended for oversight, policy enforcement, and exceptional support handling on the marketplace.

The targeted record belongs to the shopping mall order item domain, where each item has its own lifecycle independent of the rest of the order. When the forced cancellation is accepted, the item is moved to the cancelled state and the stock tied to the purchased variant is restored through the inventory flow. If the item has already been finalized by another completed action, the system must reject the duplicate intervention and keep the previous final state unchanged.

This operation is restricted to administrators. Customers and sellers must not use it, because it bypasses the normal cancellation workflow and directly applies a platform-level decision. The endpoint should be used together with order and item detail APIs when an administrator needs to inspect the current item state before taking action.
operations.name: forceCancel
operations.specification:
Load the target order item by orderItemId and verify it exists. Confirm the caller is an authenticated administrator.

Check the current item status and finalization state before applying any update. If the item is already in a finalized state caused by a prior cancellation, refund, or other completed enforcement action, reject the request as a duplicate intervention and leave the record unchanged.

If the item is eligible, perform the force-cancel in a transaction: update the order item status to cancelled, record the enforcement outcome on the item record if the schema supports such state tracking, and restore the purchased quantity back into inventory for the associated product variant. Ensure inventory restoration is consistent with the item quantity, and do not touch unrelated order items in the same order.

Return the updated order item after the transaction commits. Handle not-found, unauthorized, forbidden, and conflict-style duplicate-action cases explicitly. No request payload is required because the operation is fully determined by the path parameter and administrator privileges.

operations.description:
Force-refund a single order item as an administrative enforcement action.

This operation is used when a platform administrator needs to override the ordinary refund workflow and finalize a refund for one purchased line item. The target is a single record in the order item table, not the entire order, because the platform keeps fulfillment and dispute state at the item level. The order item record stores the purchased variant, quantity, item status, and the timestamps that mark lifecycle changes such as shipping, delivery, cancellation, and refund completion.

The refund decision must be recorded for audit and dispute review. The implementation should preserve the refund-request history when present, and should create the necessary snapshot/history entries so the enforcement decision can be reconstructed later. If the order item is already in a final state because of another completed action, the request must be rejected and the previous final state must remain unchanged.

When the refund is applied successfully, the item status becomes refunded and the affected variant stock must be restored through an inventory movement record. The stock change must be appended to inventory history rather than directly mutating the current stock state, because the platform reconstructs stock from movement records. The action must not affect other items in the same order, and the parent order should continue to follow its own lifecycle rules after the item-level refund is completed.

This endpoint is available only to administrators. It is part of the platform oversight and enforcement tools used to resolve disputes or apply policy decisions on a specific purchased item. Clients should use the order item identifier in the path to target exactly one line item, and the request body may include an administrative reason or note to preserve the justification for the enforcement record.
operations.name: forceRefund
operations.specification:
Load the target order item by id and verify it exists.
Confirm the caller has administrator privileges.

Validate that the item is eligible for administrative refund enforcement. If the item is already finalized by another completed action, reject the request as a duplicate intervention and return a conflict-style error. Do not modify any data when the target is already finalized.

Within a transaction, update the order item status to refunded and set refunded_at to the current timestamp if not already set. If the item has an associated refund request or request snapshot trail, preserve the refund enforcement decision by creating the appropriate history/snapshot record with the admin reason or note.

Restore inventory for the purchased variant by inserting a positive inventory record with the refunded quantity, using a reason such as administrative force refund. The restoration must be append-only and derived from the order item quantity. Do not directly edit current stock values.

If the parent order’s aggregate state needs recomputation, recalculate it after the item update so the order reflects the new mix of item statuses. Ensure other order items remain untouched. Return an appropriate success response or the updated item representation according to the generated API contract.

operations.description:
Retrieve the pending seller approval queue for administrative review.

This operation returns seller registration requests that are still in the pending state so an administrator can inspect applications awaiting approval or rejection. It is intended for queue browsing and review work, not for making a decision directly. The underlying source of truth is the `shopping_mall_seller_approval_requests` table, whose status column tracks whether each request is pending, approved, or rejected, and whose `rejection_reason` column stores the reason only when a request has been rejected.

The response is designed for administrators who manage seller approval records. It should surface enough information to identify the applicant, review the current state of the request, and sort or page through the queue efficiently. The immutable review history stored in `shopping_mall_seller_approval_request_reviews` is related data, but it is not the primary payload for this endpoint; the history is used when administrators need to inspect prior decision events separately.

Only pending requests are returned by this endpoint. Requests that have already been approved or rejected must not appear here, because resolved requests cannot be processed again and the pending queue must remain a clean worklist for current decisions. If a seller submits another registration attempt after rejection, that creates a new pending request record rather than changing the resolved one, so the queue continues to represent only active items requiring review.

The request supports pagination, sorting, and optional search-style filtering so administrators can browse large approval queues without loading all rows at once. Results should be ordered in a way that is useful for moderation, typically by creation time with the newest or oldest pending requests first depending on the requested sort criteria. This endpoint should return a paginated summary view rather than full entity details to keep the queue efficient for list rendering and to encourage a separate detail operation when deeper inspection is required.
operations.name: index
operations.specification:
Implement a seller approval request queue query against shopping_mall_seller_approval_requests with a fixed status predicate of pending. Join only what is necessary for summary presentation, primarily the seller identifier/reference from the request row; do not load approval review history unless the detail workflow explicitly requires it.

Accept a request body with pagination, search, and sorting inputs. Enforce administrator-only authorization at the route or service layer. Apply filtering so only rows where status = 'pending' are returned, and exclude any record that has already been resolved. Respect the unique seller constraint on shopping_mall_seller_approval_requests so that the queue reflects at most one active pending request per seller.

Sort the results deterministically, preferably by created_at and id as a tiebreaker. Return a paginated collection of summary items with fields sufficient for queue browsing: request id, seller id, status, rejection reason if present, created_at, and updated_at. Since this endpoint is read-only and does not alter the workflow state, no transaction is required beyond standard read consistency.

Handle empty results by returning an empty page payload rather than an error. Validate all pagination inputs and reject invalid page sizes or malformed sort keys. Keep the response aligned with the list-summary pattern used across the service so the UI can render the pending review table efficiently.

operations.description:
Retrieve the paginated queue of pending administrator application requests for super administrator review.

This endpoint exposes the governance inbox for administrator elevation requests stored in the administrator request table. Each returned item represents a request whose current status is still pending and therefore eligible for review according to the platform's administrator request rules. The response is designed for super administrators who need to inspect the applicant's reason, identify whether the application was submitted by a customer or a seller, and decide which request should be opened for review next.

The request data comes from the canonical administrator request record and its normalized applicant subtype link tables. The request row provides the current application state, the applicant-provided reason, and the timestamp metadata used for queue ordering. The applicant subtype records provide the source actor identity so the review interface can distinguish customer-submitted applications from seller-submitted applications without relying on nullable foreign keys in the main request table. Review history itself is preserved separately in the administrator request review table, which allows this list endpoint to remain focused on the pending review queue while still supporting later audit and decision tracking.

Only super administrators may access this operation. Regular administrators and applicants must not be able to enumerate pending governance requests. The endpoint should support pagination, search, and sorting so that the queue can be handled in operational order, typically newest first or by submission time, while still allowing filtering by applicant type or keyword matching against the request reason. Requests that are no longer pending must be excluded from this list, and the response should reflect only records that are currently eligible for review.
operations.name: index
operations.specification:
Implement a paginated pending-request listing service for administrator governance review.

Query shopping_mall_administrator_requests with status = 'pending' only. Join or load applicant linkage from shopping_mall_administrator_request_applicant_customers and shopping_mall_administrator_request_applicant_sellers to determine the applicant actor type and identity. Sort by created_at descending by default, and support additional sorting and keyword search on reason, plus optional applicant-type filtering. Because the endpoint is a list/search operation, accept request body criteria rather than query-string-only parameters.

Return a page container of summary DTOs. Each summary item should include the request id, reason, status, created_at, applicant kind, and a compact applicant identity reference. Do not include review decisions as part of the list payload unless they are needed for row-level UI cues; if included, derive them from shopping_mall_administrator_request_reviews without mutating the request state. Use read-only transaction semantics and avoid locking unless the implementation needs a consistent snapshot for pagination.

Enforce authorization so only super administrators can invoke it. If the authenticated actor is not a super administrator, reject with forbidden. If pagination parameters are invalid, reject with validation errors. If no pending requests exist, return an empty page rather than an error. The endpoint must never return approved or rejected requests.

DTO naming should follow the project prefix convention, using ShoppingMall as the prefix in component types. The request body should represent list criteria, and the response should be a paginated summary collection suitable for the review inbox UI.

operations.description:
Retrieve the grade-change history for a specific administrator account.

This operation returns the immutable audit trail of administrator grade transitions associated with the administrator identified by the path parameter. It exists so super administrators can review when an administrator was promoted from regular administrator to super administrator or demoted back to regular administrator, supporting the platform’s governance and auditability requirements.

The history is part of the administrator-grade workflow where only super administrators may manage grades. Because this record is preserved for accountability, this endpoint is read-only and does not create, update, or delete any history rows. The newest grade-change events should be listed first so reviewers can quickly understand the latest governance actions and the current administrative state.

Access to this endpoint should be restricted to super administrators, since ordinary administrators do not have authority over administrator grade management. The endpoint is typically used together with the grade management operations that actually perform promotions and demotions, while this endpoint serves as the audit view that exposes those recorded outcomes.

If the target administrator does not exist, the service should return the normal not-found response. If the administrator exists but has no grade history yet, the service should still succeed and return an empty paginated collection.

Do not derive history from the current administrator grade field; only return persisted history rows.

access.description:

This token must be included in the Authorization header using the Bearer
scheme (e.g., `Authorization: Bearer {access}`) for all endpoints requiring

instruction:
# E-Commerce Shopping Mall Platform

I want to create an e-commerce shopping mall platform.

## Customer Account

- This platform requires registration to use any features (no guest browsing)
- Customers sign up with email and password
- Customers log in with email and password
- Customers can change their password
- Customers can delete their account
- When a customer deletes their account:
  - Their profile information is deleted
  - Their orders and order history are preserved (for seller records and legal purposes)
  - Their reviews are preserved but shown as "deleted user"

## Customer Profile

- Each customer has a profile with: display name and phone number
- Customers can edit their display name and phone number

## Address Management

- Customers can add multiple shipping addresses
- Each address has: recipient name, phone number, street address, city, state/province, postal code, country
- Customers can edit their addresses
- Customers can delete their addresses
- Customers can set one address as the default shipping address

## Seller Account

- Sellers sign up with email and password
- Sellers log in with email and password
- Sellers can change their password
- Seller accounts require administrator approval before they can sell
- Sellers can view their approval status (pending, approved, rejected)
- If rejected, sellers can view the rejection reason
- Rejected sellers can submit a new registration request
- Sellers can delete their account only if:
  - They have no pending orders (paid or shipped status)
  - They have no pending cancellation or refund requests
- When a seller deletes their account:
  - Their products are deleted from listings
  - Order history and snapshots are preserved
  - Their shop name in past orders is preserved

## Seller Profile

- Each seller has a profile with: shop name, shop description, and logo image
- Sellers can edit their shop name, description, and logo
- Every edit creates a snapshot
- Customers can view seller profiles

## Categories

- Products are organized into categories
- Categories can have subcategories (one level of nesting only)
- Each category has: name and description
- Categories are created and managed by administrators only
- Customers can browse the list of all categories
- Customers can view products within a category

## Snapshot Principle

- This is a platform where money is exchanged, so all data modifications must be recorded
- Whenever editable data is modified, a snapshot is created to preserve the previous state
- Snapshots record: when the change was made, what was changed, and the values before and after
- Snapshots are immutable and cannot be deleted
- Snapshots can be viewed by relevant parties (owners, administrators) for dispute resolution

**Product Snapshot Structure**
- When a product is edited, a product snapshot is created
- The product snapshot includes all product fields (name, description, category, base price, images)
- The product snapshot also includes snapshots of all variants at that moment (product-snapshot → product-snapshot-SKU)
- This preserves the complete state of a product and its variants at any point in time

**Snapshot applies to:**
- Products (all fields including images)
- Product variants (SKU code, option values, price)
- Seller profiles (shop name, description, logo)
- Order items (product, variant, and seller profile at time of purchase)
- Reviews (rating, text content)
- Cancellation requests (reason, status changes)
- Refund requests (reason, status changes)

## Products

- Sellers can create products
- Every product has:
  - Name (required)
  - Description (required)
  - Category (required, can select a subcategory)
  - Base price (required)
- Products belong to the seller who created them
- Sellers can edit their own products
- Every edit creates a snapshot
- Sellers can delete their own products only if:
  - There are no pending order items (paid or shipped status) for any variant of the product
  - There are no pending cancellation or refund requests for any variant of the product
- Deleting a product also deletes all its variants and inventory records
- Deleted products no longer appear in search or category listings
- Sellers can view snapshots of their own products
- Administrators can view snapshots of any product
- Snapshots are preserved even after product deletion

## Product Images

- Sellers can upload multiple images for each product
- Images can be reordered (first image is the main/thumbnail image)
- Sellers can delete images from their products
- Image changes are included in product snapshots

## Product Variants (SKU)

- A product can have multiple variants
- Each variant represents a specific combination of options (e.g., "Red / Large", "Blue / Small")
- Each variant has:
  - SKU code (unique identifier, required)
  - Option values (e.g., color: "Red", size: "Large")
  - Price (can override the base price, optional)
  - Stock quantity (required, starts at 0)
- Sellers can add variants to their products
- Sellers can edit variants (SKU code, option values, price)
- Every variant edit creates a snapshot
- Sellers can delete variants only if:
  - There are no pending order items (paid or shipped status) for that variant
  - There are no pending cancellation or refund requests for that variant
- A product must have at least one variant to be purchasable
- Products with no variants are visible in search but shown as "unavailable"

## Inventory Management

- Each variant has its own stock quantity
- Stock quantity is managed through inventory history records (not snapshots)
- Each inventory record contains: quantity change (positive for restocking, negative for orders/adjustments), reason, and timestamp
- Current stock is calculated by summing all inventory records
- Sellers can add inventory (restock) with a quantity and reason
- Sellers can subtract inventory (adjustment/loss) with a quantity and reason
- Order placement automatically creates a negative inventory record
- Order cancellation/refund automatically creates a positive inventory record
- Sellers can view the full inventory history of each variant
- When stock reaches 0, the variant is shown as "out of stock"
- Out of stock variants cannot be added to cart

## Product Search

- Customers can search products by name
- Search results show products from all sellers
- Search results are paginated
- Customers can filter search results by:
  - Category
  - Price range (minimum and maximum)
  - In-stock only
- Customers can sort search results by:
  - Newest first
  - Price (low to high)
  - Price (high to low)

## Product Listing

- When viewing a list of products (search results, category page), each product shows:
  - Main image (thumbnail)
  - Name
  - Base price (or price range if variants have different prices)
  - Seller shop name
  - Average rating (if reviews exist)

## Product Detail Page

- Customers can view a single product's full details
- The page shows:
  - All images
  - Name and description
  - Category
  - Seller shop name (links to seller profile)
  - All available variants with prices and stock status
  - Average rating and total review count
  - All reviews

## Wishlist

- Customers can add products to their wishlist
- Customers can view their wishlist
- The wishlist is paginated
- Wishlist shows products (not specific variants)
- Customers can remove products from their wishlist
- If a product is deleted by the seller, it is automatically removed from all wishlists

## Shopping Cart

- Customers can add variants to their cart (must select a specific variant, not just a product)
- When adding to cart, customers specify the quantity
- If the same variant is already in the cart, the quantities are combined (not added as a separate line)
- Customers can view their cart
- Cart shows each item with: product name, variant options, price, quantity, and subtotal
- Customers can change the quantity of items in their cart
- Customers can remove items from their cart
- Cart shows the total price of all items
- If a variant's stock is less than the cart quantity, a warning is shown
- If a variant is deleted or out of stock, it is marked as unavailable in the cart

## Checkout

- Customers can proceed to checkout from their cart
- Unavailable items cannot be checked out
- Customers must select a shipping address (or use default)
- Customers can review the order summary before placing the order:
  - List of items with prices
  - Shipping address
  - Total price
- Once an order is placed, the shipping address cannot be changed

## Payment

- After reviewing, customers confirm and place the order
- Payment is processed (assume external payment gateway integration)
- Payment can succeed or fail
- If payment fails, the order is not created and customers can retry
- If payment succeeds, the order is created

## Order Creation

- When an order is placed successfully:
  - Stock quantities are decreased for each purchased variant
  - Items are removed from the customer's cart
  - An order record is created
  - Each purchased variant becomes an order item with status "paid"
  - A snapshot of each purchased product and variant is saved with the order item (preserves product name, description, variant options, and price at the time of purchase)
  - A snapshot of each seller's profile is saved with the order item (preserves shop name and logo at the time of purchase)

## Order Structure

- An order contains one or more order items
- Each order item represents a purchased product variant with a quantity
- If a customer buys 3 of the same variant, it becomes one order item with quantity 3
- Order items can be from different sellers
- Each order item has its own status
- Each order item can be individually cancelled or refunded
- Order items are grouped into shipments when shipped (see Shipping and Tracking)

## Order History

- Customers can view a list of all their orders
- The list is paginated and sorted by newest first
- Each order in the list shows: order number, date, total price, and overall order status
- Customers can view the full details of an order:
  - List of items with: product name, variant, quantity, price, and item status
  - Shipping address
  - List of shipments with tracking information (each shipment shows which items are included)

## Order Status

**Order Item Status**
- Each item in an order has its own status
- Item statuses:
  - Paid: payment completed, waiting for seller to ship
  - Shipped: seller has shipped the item
  - Delivered: item has been delivered
  - Cancelled: item was cancelled
  - Refunded: item was refunded

**Order Status**
- The overall order status is derived from its items
- If all items are paid → order is "paid"
- If any item is shipped (and none delivered yet) → order is "shipped"
- If all items are delivered → order is "delivered"
- If all items are cancelled → order is "cancelled"
- If all items are refunded → order is "refunded"
- Mixed states (e.g., some delivered, some refunded) → order is "partially completed"

## Shipping and Tracking

**Shipment Concept**
- A shipment is a package sent by a seller
- A shipment can contain one or more order items from the same seller
- Different sellers always ship separately (different shipments)
- A seller can choose to ship items individually or bundle multiple items into one shipment

**Shipping Process**
- Sellers can view order items for their products that need shipping
- When shipping, sellers select one or more of their items to include in a shipment
- Sellers enter tracking information for the shipment (carrier name, tracking number)
- All items in the same shipment share the same tracking information
- When a shipment is created, all items in it change to status "shipped"

**Delivery Confirmation**
- Customers can view tracking information for each shipment
- Customers confirm delivery per shipment (not per item)
- When the customer confirms delivery, all items in that shipment change to status "delivered"
- If the customer does not confirm, items automatically change to "delivered" after 14 days from shipping

## Order Cancellation

- Cancellation is handled per order item, not per entire order
- Customers can request cancellation for individual items with status "paid" (not yet shipped)
- Cancellation requests include a reason (text)
- The seller of that item can approve or reject the cancellation request
- When a seller responds, a snapshot of the request state is created
- If approved, that item is cancelled and refund is processed for that item only
- Cancelled items restore their stock quantities (via inventory record)
- The remaining items in the order continue processing normally
- If all items in an order are cancelled, the entire order status becomes "cancelled"

## Refund Requests

- Refund is handled per order item, not per entire order
- Customers can request a refund for individual items with status "delivered"
- Refund requests include a reason (text)
- Refund can be requested within 7 days of that item being delivered
- The seller of that item can approve or reject the refund request
- When a seller responds, a snapshot of the request state is created
- If approved, that item is refunded
- Refunded items restore their stock quantities (via inventory record)
- The remaining items in the order are unaffected
- If all items in an order are refunded, the entire order status becomes "refunded"

## Reviews and Ratings

- Customers can write a review for products they have purchased
- A review can only be written after that item's status is "delivered"
- Customers can write one review per product per order
- Each review has:
  - Rating (1 to 5 stars, required)
  - Text content (optional)
- Reviews are displayed on the product detail page
- Reviews are sorted by newest first
- Customers can edit their own reviews
- Every review edit creates a snapshot
- Customers can delete their own reviews (but snapshots are preserved)
- Product's average rating is calculated from all non-deleted reviews

## Seller Dashboard

- Sellers can view a summary of their shop:
  - Total number of products
  - Total number of order items (for their products)
  - Number of pending cancellation requests
  - Number of pending refund requests
- Sellers can view a list of all order items for their products
- Sellers can filter order items by status

## Administrator System

**Becoming an Administrator**
- Any user (customer or seller) can submit a request to become an administrator
- The request includes a reason (text)
- Super administrators can view the list of pending requests
- Super administrators can approve or reject requests
- When approved, the user becomes a regular administrator

**Administrator Grades**
- There are two grades: regular administrator and super administrator
- Super administrators can promote regular administrators to super administrator
- Super administrators can demote other super administrators to regular administrator
- Super administrators cannot demote themselves

**Seller Management**
- Administrators can view the list of pending seller approvals
- Administrators can approve or reject seller registrations
- When rejecting, administrators must provide a reason
- Rejected sellers can submit a new registration request
- Administrators can suspend seller accounts
- When a seller is suspended:
  - Their products are hidden from search and category listings
  - Their products cannot be purchased
  - They can still process existing orders (ship items, respond to cancellation/refund requests)
  - They cannot create new products or edit existing products
- Administrators can unsuspend seller accounts (products become visible again)

**Category Management**
- Administrators can create categories and subcategories
- Administrators can edit category names and descriptions
- Administrators can delete categories (products in deleted categories become uncategorized)

**Product Oversight**
- Administrators can view all products on the platform
- Administrators can view snapshots of any product
- Administrators can delete any product (for policy violations)

**Order Oversight**
- Administrators can view all orders on the platform
- Administrators can force-cancel individual items or entire orders (refunds the customer, restores stock)
- Administrators can force-refund individual items or entire orders

**User Management**
- Administrators can view all customer accounts
- Administrators can ban customers (banned customers cannot log in)
- Administrators can unban customers
- Administrators can view all seller accounts
- Administrators can ban sellers (banned sellers cannot log in, existing orders remain)

dependencies.purpose: Authenticate as the target customer because the endpoint requires a customer session before account-state restrictions can be evaluated.

functions.name: test_api_customer_email_verification_banned_account_access

scenario.draft: Verify a signed-in customer can change their own password through the password-reset workflow when the request is authorized and the current password matches. The test should confirm the endpoint accepts the correct account family, updates only the password credential, and returns the updated customer identity summary. After the change, confirm the customer can authenticate with the new password and the old password no longer works. Also verify the customer account state itself is unchanged, including status and profile-related data, and that the password reset record is marked as consumed in the returned workflow state.

dependencies.purpose: Register a customer account so there is an authenticated identity available for the password change flow.

functions.name: test_api_customer_password_reset_success

scenario.draft: Verify password change is rejected when the current password verification does not match the authenticated customer’s existing credential. The test should exercise the business rule that the account owner must prove possession of the current password before a change is accepted. Confirm the customer’s password remains unchanged, the account remains active, and no session or profile data is modified. This scenario should validate the security boundary rather than any input-shape behavior.

dependencies.purpose: Register a customer account so the test can attempt a real password change against an existing identity.

functions.name: test_api_customer_password_reset_current_password_mismatch

scenario.draft: Verify the endpoint prevents reuse of an already-consumed password reset token. The test should first obtain a valid password reset state, complete one successful password change, then attempt to submit the same reset credential again. Confirm the second attempt is rejected, the account password stays at the first new value, and the reset token is not processed twice. This protects the one-time-use rule and ensures the password reset workflow remains idempotent with respect to token reuse.

dependencies.purpose: Register a customer account so a real password reset workflow can be exercised.

functions.name: test_api_customer_password_reset_token_reuse_rejected

scenario.draft: Verify that an authenticated customer can retrieve an existing password reset record by ID and receive the full persisted record shape, including the owning customer summary and lifecycle timestamps. Confirm the response reflects the current state of the token record without changing it: the record remains usable/expired/used exactly as stored, and repeated reads return the same data. Validate that the returned customer summary exposes only safe account identity fields and does not alter account state or consume the reset token.

dependencies.purpose: Authenticate as a customer because this endpoint is restricted to the customer actor.

functions.name: test_api_customer_password_reset_retrieve

scenario.draft: Verify that requesting a password reset record that does not exist is handled as a missing-resource case for the active account-recovery workflow. The test should confirm the endpoint does not reveal any other password reset data, does not create a new token, and does not mutate existing recovery state. This scenario protects the sensitive token lookup path by ensuring only the exact persisted record can be read.

dependencies.purpose: Authenticate as a customer because access to password reset records is restricted to the customer actor.

functions.name: test_api_customer_password_reset_not_found

scenario.draft: Verify that an authenticated customer can retrieve an existing password reset record and that the endpoint returns the preserved record state without modifying it. The test should confirm the response is read-only by performing the same GET request twice and comparing the returned details for consistency. If the record already contains lifecycle timestamps such as usedAt or expiredAt, the response should expose them unchanged rather than consuming, renewing, or mutating the token. The scenario should avoid assuming any setup flow for creating or expiring the record unless such a prerequisite is available in the interface.

dependencies.purpose: Authenticate as a customer because the endpoint is restricted to the customer actor.

functions.name: test_api_customer_password_reset_preserved_state

scenario.draft: Verify that an authenticated customer can retrieve only their own session history in a paginated list, with the newest sessions returned first by default. Authenticate the customer, then call the endpoint with standard pagination criteria. Assert that each returned row contains only the customer's own session records and that no session belonging to another account appears. Confirm the response is paginated correctly, the default order is newest-first, and the endpoint behaves correctly when the customer has no prior session history beyond the current authenticated session, returning an empty or single-item page as appropriate rather than an error.

dependencies.purpose: Authenticate as the customer whose session history will be listed.

functions.name: test_api_customer_sessions_list_own_history

scenario.draft: Verify that the authenticated customer's session list is paginated correctly and remains scoped to the caller's own account. First authenticate by joining as a customer. Then seed enough sessions for that same customer with different connection metadata and creation times. Request a middle page using a small page size, and validate that the returned pagination metadata matches the requested paging criteria and total record count. Confirm that the response records are limited to the authenticated customer's sessions, and that the ordering follows the endpoint's defined session-list sorting behavior. Also verify that filtering by session metadata returns only matching sessions within the same account scope.

dependencies.purpose: Authenticate as the customer who owns the sessions being inspected.

functions.name: test_api_customer_sessions_paginated_searchable_list

scenario.draft: Verify that an inactive or banned customer cannot use the session listing endpoint even if a session exists historically. Set up a customer account, then arrange the account state so it is no longer permitted to use platform sessions. When the customer attempts to retrieve session history, the system should reject access before returning any session data. The test should confirm that no cross-account or stale session information is exposed and that the response is an access-state or authorization failure rather than a normal page of results.

dependencies.purpose: Authenticate as the customer account used to verify access control before the account is placed into a blocked state.

functions.name: test_api_customer_sessions_blocked_for_inactive_account

scenario.draft: Verify that an authenticated customer can retrieve their own session details by sessionId and receives the full read model needed for session-security screens: session id, owning customer summary, IP, href, referrer, createdAt, and expiredAt. Confirm the returned customer summary matches the signed-in customer and that the session metadata reflects the stored creation context. Also verify that the operation remains read-only and does not change the session state. As an important access-boundary check, attempt to retrieve another customer's session from the same customer account and confirm the request is rejected because the session is outside the caller's own account scope. Include a case where the owning customer account is no longer active (for example deleted or otherwise disabled) and confirm the session can still be inspected for security/audit purposes by the owner, while the session is treated as unusable for authenticated features downstream.

dependencies.purpose: Authenticate as a registered customer so the session endpoint can be exercised within the correct actor boundary.

functions.name: test_api_customer_session_read_own_and_access_boundary

scenario.draft: Validate the session detail view used for account security management by checking that the endpoint returns a precise snapshot of a known customer session, including the correct owner identity and the stored connection metadata. The test should confirm the response exposes the session's creation timestamp and expiration timestamp so clients can determine whether the session is still valid. It should also verify that the response does not mutate any data, since this endpoint is informational only. This scenario focuses on the business meaning of the session record as an authentication artifact rather than customer commerce data, ensuring the returned owner summary and metadata are consistent and complete for security review.

dependencies.purpose: Authenticate as a registered customer to create the security context required for reading customer session data.

functions.name: test_api_customer_session_security_detail_view

scenario.draft: As an authenticated customer, retrieve a single session record that belongs to the current account and verify that the response exposes the session owner identity and connection metadata for security review. Confirm that the endpoint returns the expected preserved session details for the authenticated owner, and that the scenario stays within the account’s active session-management boundary. Include coverage for the normal readable case and the unauthorized-access boundary by ensuring only the session owner can inspect the session record.

dependencies.purpose: Authenticate as a registered customer before inspecting the customer's own session record.

functions.name: test_api_customer_session_inspection

scenario.draft: Verify that an authenticated administrator can retrieve a paginated seller directory with the default browsing behavior. Start by creating an administrator session, then seed multiple seller accounts with different approval states and account states, including at least one seller with a linked storefront profile and one seller without a profile. Call the seller list endpoint with standard paging and sorting controls. Assert that the response returns a stable paginated summary, includes the seller identity fields plus approval/account status, and exposes storefront profile summary data only when it exists. Confirm that sensitive auth data such as password hashes, tokens, or session details are not present. Also verify that the pagination metadata matches the returned page and total record count.

dependencies.purpose: Authenticate as an administrator because the directory is restricted to administrator access.

functions.name: test_api_administrator_seller_directory_pagination

scenario.draft: Verify seller directory browsing for administrators across approval-status, account-status, and keyword-based filtering. Authenticate as an administrator, prepare seller records covering approved, pending, rejected, active, suspended, and banned states, and ensure at least one seller profile shop name matches the search keyword. Call the endpoint with supported filter combinations: approval status only, account status only, and a keyword that matches either the seller email or linked shop name. Assert that each response contains only matching sellers, that the result set remains paginated, and that sorting is deterministic across repeated requests with the same filters. Confirm that non-matching sellers are excluded and that the response does not expose restricted account details.

dependencies.purpose: Authenticate as an administrator before accessing the seller directory.

functions.name: test_api_administrator_seller_directory_filtering

scenario.draft: Authenticate as an administrator, then request the administrator seller directory and verify the response is a paginated seller list that remains stable when it includes sellers with and without linked storefront profile data. Confirm that sellers without an attached seller profile still appear in the directory with the expected seller summary fields, and that the list response does not fail or lose pagination metadata because profile data is incomplete. Also verify that the final-page behavior is consistent for a small dataset and that the returned pagination information matches the page boundaries. Focus on business behavior of seller browsing and response completeness rather than invalid request values or framework-level validation.

dependencies.purpose: Authenticate as an administrator before accessing the seller management directory.

functions.name: test_api_administrator_seller_directory_missing_profile

scenario.draft: Verify that an administrator can retrieve a seller account by sellerId and receive the canonical seller identity record with the expected public account fields: id, email, approval status, rejection reason when present, account status, approval/rejection/suspension/ban timestamps, last login timestamp, and account lifecycle timestamps. The test should confirm the response represents the seller account only and does not expose authentication secrets or storefront profile data. Use an existing seller account fixture whose status has meaningful history so the returned timestamps and nullable rejection fields can be asserted against real business state.

dependencies.purpose: Authenticate as an administrator because the endpoint requires administrator-level access.

functions.name: test_api_seller_account_retrieve_by_administrator

scenario.draft: Verify that the seller account detail response correctly reflects moderation and security state for an account that has been approved, suspended, or banned. Use a seller fixture with non-default lifecycle history and confirm that the returned moderation and account-state fields preserve the stored values for approved, suspended, and banned transitions, including nulls for events that never occurred. This ensures the endpoint is suitable for administrative oversight and moderation review, not just basic identity lookup.

dependencies.purpose: Authenticate as an administrator because only privileged accounts can inspect seller moderation records.

functions.name: test_api_seller_account_moderation_state_visibility

scenario.draft: Verify access control on seller account inspection by attempting to retrieve a seller record that does not belong to the requesting seller context and confirming the operation is restricted to the account owner or an administrator. Because this endpoint is documented for administrator oversight, the test should ensure an authenticated non-owner seller cannot use it to inspect another seller's account, while a normal administrator can still retrieve the same record successfully. This protects merchant account privacy and enforces the account-level boundary separate from storefront data.

dependencies.purpose: Authenticate as an administrator to create the administrative context needed to verify the account boundary behavior.

functions.name: test_api_seller_account_owner_boundary_enforced

scenario.draft: Verify that a super administrator can retrieve the administrator roster with pagination and stable summary data. Start by authenticating as a super administrator, then call the roster endpoint with search and filter criteria that should match at least one administrator, such as filtering by grade or account status. Assert that the response is paginated, includes the expected current page metadata and total counts, and returns only lightweight administrator summary fields such as id, email, grade, accountStatus, createdAt, updatedAt, and deletedAt. Confirm that sensitive credentials or session data are not exposed. Also verify the list is ordered consistently across repeated calls with the same criteria so it can be used reliably for governance and grade-management workflows.

dependencies.purpose: Authenticate as a super administrator because this roster is restricted to super administrators only and the scenario must run under that privileged admin context.

functions.name: test_api_administrator_roster_pagination_and_summary

scenario.draft: Verify roster browsing behavior when the result set is constrained by search and filtering. Authenticate as a super administrator, then request the administrator list using a search term that targets identity text such as email, combined with grade or account-status filters that narrow the result set. Validate that only matching administrators are returned and that the pagination metadata reflects the reduced dataset correctly. Include an assertion for the empty-result case by using criteria that should match no administrators, ensuring the endpoint still returns a valid paginated response with zero records and no unexpected side effects. This scenario protects the governance workflow by confirming the roster can be used to locate the correct administrator for follow-up grade-management actions.

dependencies.purpose: Authenticate as a super administrator because roster search and filtering are admin-only governance actions.

functions.name: test_api_administrator_roster_search_filter_empty_result

scenario.draft: Verify that a regular administrator cannot access the full administrator roster. Authenticate as a regular administrator, then attempt to call the roster endpoint. Assert that access is denied and that the regular administrator cannot browse the full list or inspect other administrators through this governance endpoint. This protects the boundary between ordinary administrator authority and super administrator authority, which is especially important because the roster is used for grade management and oversight. The test should confirm that the denial occurs before any roster data is exposed.

dependencies.purpose: Authenticate as a regular administrator because the access-control boundary must be checked using a non-super administrator account.

functions.name: test_api_administrator_roster_super_admin_only_access

scenario.draft: Verify that an authenticated administrator can retrieve a single administrator account by UUID and that the response contains the public governance fields only. Cover the normal success path by using an existing administrator account, then assert the returned record includes the expected identifier, email, grade, account status, and timestamp metadata. Confirm that sensitive authentication material is not exposed. Also validate that the endpoint behaves as a standard detail lookup for administrator governance screens by returning the account even when the caller is using it for grade-management or oversight context. Finally, verify the not-found behavior when the requested administrator record does not exist, so the detail view handles missing governance records cleanly.

dependencies.purpose: Authenticate as an administrator because this endpoint is restricted to administrator actors.

functions.name: test_api_administrator_account_detail_lookup

scenario.draft: Test access control for administrator detail retrieval by attempting the lookup from the correct administrative context and from a non-authorized context. The primary assertion is that an authenticated administrator can access the endpoint, while a non-administrator caller cannot use it. Validate that the business rule limits the operation to platform governance identities and does not allow customer or seller access to administrator account records. This scenario is important because the endpoint exposes internal account and grade information used for governance, so the test should ensure the detail record remains protected from ordinary marketplace actors.

scenario.draft: Verify that the administrator detail endpoint returns the full public account lifecycle data for an account that has been soft-deleted or otherwise in an inactive lifecycle state, if such a record is retrievable by identifier. functions.name: test_api_administrator_account_deleted_record_lookup

scenario.draft: Verify that an authenticated customer can retrieve their own wishlist as a paginated list of saved products. Start by authenticating a customer and ensuring the customer has multiple wishlist entries. Request the wishlist and confirm the response includes pagination metadata, returns only entries owned by that customer, and represents each saved item at the product-summary level rather than variant-level detail. Validate that the list behavior is stable when the customer has no saved products by returning an empty page rather than an error. If the API specification explicitly filters out deleted products from wishlist results, confirm those removed catalog items do not appear in the customer's visible wishlist.

dependencies.purpose: Authenticate as a customer because wishlist access is customer-owned and requires customer authorization.

functions.name: test_api_customer_wishlist_retrieve_saved_products

scenario.draft: Verify paging and sorting behavior for a customer with a large wishlist. Create a customer account and prepare a wishlist large enough to span multiple pages. Request different pages with explicit limits and confirm the page metadata reflects the requested position, total record count, and total page count correctly. Then compare newest-first versus oldest-first results to ensure the list order changes as expected while still returning the same underlying saved products. This scenario should also confirm that repeated calls produce a stable read-only view during concurrent wishlist cleanup, so the customer sees a consistent page rather than partially removed or duplicated entries.

dependencies.purpose: Authenticate as a customer because only the wishlist owner can browse the saved product list.

functions.name: test_api_customer_wishlist_pagination_sorting

scenario.draft: Verify that wishlist browsing respects product lifecycle cleanup and does not expose deleted catalog entries. Set up a customer with at least one saved product, then have the product removed from the catalog before the wishlist is queried. Confirm the deleted product no longer appears in the returned wishlist page and that the remaining saved products are still listed normally. Also validate that the endpoint continues to return a valid empty page if deletion removes the customer's last active wishlist entry. The key business expectation is that wishlist views only show active products and never preserve links to deleted listings.

dependencies.purpose: Authenticate as a customer because wishlist visibility is limited to the owning customer session.

functions.name: test_api_customer_wishlist_deleted_product_removed

scenario.draft: Verify that an authenticated customer can retrieve the full detail of their own wishlist and see only the products currently saved in it. Also verify that the wishlist is read-only from this endpoint and that retrieving it does not modify wishlist contents or lifecycle timestamps.

dependencies.purpose: Authenticate as the customer who owns the wishlist so the detail view can be accessed under the correct account boundary.

functions.name: test_api_customer_wishlist_detail_own_wishlist

scenario.draft: Verify that a customer is prevented from reading another customer's wishlist detail. The test should authenticate a customer, attempt to fetch a wishlist that belongs to a different customer, and expect the system to reject access because the wishlist is owner-scoped personal shopping data. The response should not reveal wishlist contents, associated products, or any customer-private data. This scenario validates the ownership boundary for wishlist retrieval and protects customer browsing privacy.

dependencies.purpose: Authenticate a customer before attempting cross-account access so the authorization boundary is exercised under a real logged-in session.

functions.name: test_api_customer_wishlist_detail_other_customer_forbidden

scenario.draft: Verify that an authenticated customer can retrieve the active cart view for the signed-in account after the cart has been prepared in prerequisite setup. Register a customer first, then ensure the customer has an active cart with at least one item through explicit prerequisite cart setup. Call the cart retrieval endpoint and assert that the response returns only the authenticated customer's active cart, including the cart owner information, current line items, per-item subtotals, and the cart total. Verify that the returned payload reflects the current persisted cart state at the time of retrieval and does not expose another customer's cart data. Also confirm that pagination metadata, if returned by the endpoint, is internally consistent with the cart collection data. This scenario should cover the normal success path for viewing a populated customer cart and should not attempt to validate cart mutation behavior through this read-only endpoint.

functions.name: test_api_customer_cart_retrieve_active_cart

scenario.draft: Verify that the cart retrieval endpoint respects customer ownership and account status. Then attempt to access cart data from a different authenticated customer context and confirm the endpoint does not expose another customer's cart. Include a deleted customer account context as the critical business edge case: once the account is deleted, the cart should no longer be available as an active shopping area for that user. This scenario validates the rule that cart access is restricted to registered, active customer accounts and is not shared across accounts.

dependencies.purpose: Register the first customer who owns the target cart session.

functions.name: test_api_customer_cart_access_by_owner_only

Assert that the response follows the platform's empty-cart convention: either it returns an empty active cart representation with zero line items and zero total, or it returns the configured not-found behavior if lazy cart creation is not supported by the service. The important business check is that the operation does not fabricate product placeholders and does not expose unrelated customer data. This scenario covers the edge case of first-time cart access and confirms the endpoint is safe to call even when no purchase selections exist yet.

dependencies.purpose: Register a new customer whose cart has not yet been populated.

functions.name: test_api_customer_cart_empty_first_access
